newsitem.title: USA: Waigel beats EMU drum for U.S. business leaders.
newsitem.headline: Waigel beats EMU drum for U.S. business leaders.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Tuesday told business leaders he was confident Germany would make the grade for Europe's single currency and that the euro would be an anchor for other countries as well.

In the text of a speech prepared for delivery to the German-American Chamber of Commerce in New York, Waigel said Bonn's target of 2.5 percent economic growth this year was realistic and that monetary union would begin on time.

"We are moving in the right direction regarding budget policies," Waigel said according to the text of his speech. "I am confident that we will force our total public deficit this year down to three percent of gross domestic product."

The Maastricht treaty on European economic and monetary union (EMU) sets a range of economic requirements that must be met in 1997 and which the European Union will use to decide which of its members qualifies for EMU's first wave in 1999.
The most important target, and the one many countries are having the most difficulty meeting, is the restriction of deficits to three percent of GDP.
Germany, dangerously close to missing the deficit criterion, was back on the track of economic growth, Waigel said. "A rise in domestic product of 2.5 percent this year is realistic."

Turning to the importance of monetary union, Waigel said that although the criteria were tough, it was crucial to observe them strictly or else run the risk of losing the confidence of financial markets.

"That is why the basic principle is important to me from the beginning: convergence determines the timetable and not the other way around," he said. "But I am still certain that monetary union will begin on time."

The new European currency will improve the chances of European companies to compete on global markets and will also contribute to stabilising the world economy and the relationship to the dollar, he said.
"It will become an anchor currency for all non-European countries and contribute decisively to the competitiveness of European financial and capital markets," Waigel said.
But he warned that there would be considerable consequences should EMU collapse.
"With fair certainty there would be turbulence on financial markets, whereby flight into the Deutschmark could be accompanied by a particularly negative impact on exports and jobs," he said.
The failure of Europe's most ambitious project could also "endanger the eastward expansion of the EU and with it the opening of new markets," he added.
